content.title: About
content.content: Dry nonfat milk is a dairy product from which most of the water and virtually all fat have been removed. After drying, it can be quickly reconstituted by adding water, producing a beverage close in taste and nutrition to fresh milk. The product is convenient for long‑term storage and transport, and is widely used in the food industry and households.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry milk was first produced in the early 20th century to ensure food security during wars.
Nonfat dry milk contains about 35 % protein, making it a rich source of amino acids.
Reconstituted dry milk retains most B‑vitamins but is sensitive to light and heat.
It is commonly used in infant formulas, sports nutrition, and bakery products.
Spray drying is the typical method: milk is atomized into fine droplets that instantly evaporate.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Nonfat dry milk provides roughly 35 % protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The near‑absence of fat makes it suitable for low‑calorie and low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: It retains a high calcium content, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Reconstituted milk supplies riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient storage
items.content: Lack of moisture allows long shelf life without refrigeration, useful for travel and emergency kits.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Vitamin loss with improper storage
items.content: Extended exposure to heat or light can degrade vitamins A and D.

items.title: Excess protein intake
items.content: Very high consumption may strain kidneys in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: To reconstitute, mix 1 part dry milk with 4–5 parts cold water and stir until smooth. The resulting liquid can be drunk as milk, added to cereals, smoothies, baked goods, sauces, or infant formulas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry milk in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. After opening, use within 3–6 months. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or signs of mold.
